# A Prompt Framework for Marketers: RTCROS, With Examples You Can Copy

URL: https://aiinmarketing.in/blogs/rtcros-prompt-framework-for-marketers
Author: Kailas Nath R
Co-author: Kautilya Roshan
Published: 2026-11-04
Summary: Learn RTCROS, a six-part prompt framework (Role, Task, Context, Rules, Output format, Style) with marketing examples, plus a free branded PDF guide.

Most marketers do not get poor results from AI because the tool is weak. They get them because the prompt reads like a text to a friend: "write an ad for my class". This guide gives you a six-part prompt framework for marketers, RTCROS, with copy-ready examples for ads, SEO, WhatsApp follow-ups and weekly reports.

**Key takeaways**

- RTCROS stands for Role, Task, Context, Rules, Output format and Style. It is a checklist you run before you press enter, not a magic formula.
- RTCROS is our own working checklist, not an industry standard. Other frameworks, such as CO-STAR from GovTech Singapore, cover similar ground, and the guide shows how they map to each other.
- Anthropic's own prompting guide gives a simple test: show your prompt to a colleague with no background and see if they would be confused. If they would be, the AI will be too.
- Four ready prompts are included for Meta ad review, an SEO brief, a WhatsApp follow-up and a weekly numbers read, each with the six parts labelled.
- A free 3-page PDF with the template, the examples and a checklist is below, branded for AIM by Adsmentor.

## Why most prompts disappoint

Picture a new intern on day one. You say, "Write an ad for my yoga class." They would have questions: for whom, where will it run, what is the offer, what is the budget, what can we not say? An AI tool cannot ask those questions unless you invite it to, so it guesses, and guesses sound generic.

Anthropic, the company behind Claude, describes a useful check in its [prompting best practices](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices). Its "key test" is to show your prompt to a colleague with minimal context on the task and ask them to follow it. In the guide's words, if they would be confused, Claude will be too. That one test explains most weak AI output in marketing.

A framework turns the test into a habit. You do not need to memorise theory. You need six boxes you fill in every time.

## RTCROS in one minute

RTCROS is the checklist we teach at AIM. To be clear about its status: it is not a published standard, and it is not tied to one tool. You will meet other acronyms with similar letters online, and the order of the letters matters far less than covering the six jobs.

| Letter | Question it answers | Weak version | Stronger version |
|---|---|---|---|
| **R**ole | Who should the AI act as? | (nothing) | "You are a senior performance marketer who coaches beginners." |
| **T**ask | What exactly is the job? | "Help with my ad" | "Review the Meta ad below and find its three weakest points." |
| **C**ontext | What does it need to know that it cannot guess? | (nothing) | "Weekend yoga workshop, Pune, working women 28 to 40, goal 50 sign-ups." |
| **R**ules | What must it do, and never do? | (nothing) | "Do not invent statistics. Flag any claim that could break ad policy." |
| **O**utput format | What shape should the answer take? | "Give me ideas" | "A table: issue, why it matters, one fix." |
| **S**tyle | How should it sound? | (nothing) | "Plain English, warm, under 150 words, no jargon." |

Read down the "weak" column and you will see most of the prompts you have written so far. The good news is that the fix costs about two minutes.

## The six parts, one by one

### Role: point the AI at the right kind of thinking

A role is a short sentence that focuses the answer. Anthropic's guide says setting a role in the system prompt focuses the model's behaviour and tone, and that even a single sentence makes a difference. For marketers, think of the person you would hire for the job: a copywriter for Indian D2C brands, an SEO editor, a CRM specialist. Name the helper and, if it matters, who the answer is for: "explain to a shop owner with no marketing background".

### Task: one verb, one deliverable

Good tasks start with a verb and name the thing you will receive: "Rewrite", "Review", "List", "Compare", "Draft three versions". If you want two jobs done, make two prompts or number the steps. A prompt that asks for strategy, copy and a report in one go gets a little of each and not enough of any.

### Context: the facts it cannot guess

Context is where your knowledge enters. Include the business, the audience, the goal, the numbers you already have, the offer, the channel and what you tried before. Paste real text, for example last month's best ad, instead of describing it. Leave out private data you should not share, such as customer phone numbers.

### Rules: fences, not decoration

Rules are the do and do-not list. Useful rules for marketers include: use only the facts I gave you, do not invent numbers or testimonials, keep claims inside advertising policy, avoid words I have banned, ask me a question if something is missing. A rule that says "ask me before guessing" prevents many confident mistakes.

### Output format: decide the shape before you read it

Ask for the format you will actually use: a table you can paste into a sheet, five options numbered, a headline under 40 characters, a checklist. If the output will go into another tool, say so. Anthropic's guide also suggests using XML-style tags such as <context> and <input> when a prompt mixes instructions with pasted material, because wrapping each type of content in its own tag reduces misinterpretation.

### Style: voice and reading level

Style is the sound of the answer: warm or formal, plain English or Hinglish, short sentences, no jargon, the brand's voice. Pasting two or three samples of your brand's writing and saying "match this voice" is more reliable than adjectives alone. The same guide notes that a few well-crafted examples, known as few-shot or multishot prompting, improve accuracy and consistency.

## One prompt, built step by step

Here is the idea in action. The scenario is an example brief we made up for teaching, not a real client: a weekend yoga workshop in Pune for working women.

**Version 1:** "Write a Facebook ad for my yoga workshop."

The result is predictable: "Unlock your inner peace!" Now add the six parts.

> **Role:** You are a senior performance copywriter who writes Meta ads for Indian small businesses.
>
> **Task:** Write three versions of primary text for a Facebook and Instagram feed ad.
>
> **Context:** A two-day weekend yoga workshop in Pune, fee ₹499, for working women aged 28 to 40 who feel stiff after desk jobs. Goal: 50 sign-ups in ten days. Trainer has taught for 8 years.
>
> **Rules:** Use only the facts above. Do not promise medical results. Do not use the words "miracle" or "cure". If a fact is missing, ask me before guessing.
>
> **Output format:** Three versions, each with a headline under 40 characters and primary text under 125 characters, in a table.
>
> **Style:** Warm, plain English, speak to one woman, no jargon.

The second prompt is longer, but you will spend less time editing, and the answer will contain things you can check against your facts. Notice the rule "if a fact is missing, ask me". It turns the AI from a guesser into a collaborator.

## Four copy-ready prompts for everyday marketing work

Swap the details in brackets for your own. Each one carries all six parts. Read the answers critically: the framework improves the first draft, it does not replace your judgement.

### 1. Review a Meta ad before it goes live

> **Role:** You are a paid social reviewer who checks ads the way a strict client would.
>
> **Task:** Review the ad copy below and list the three weakest points.
>
> **Context:** [Business, audience, offer, goal, budget]. The ad copy is inside the tags: <ad>paste copy here</ad>.
>
> **Rules:** Do not rewrite the ad. Ask me one question per weak point. Flag any claim that could break Meta ad policy.
>
> **Output format:** A table with three columns: weak point, why it matters, question for me.
>
> **Style:** Direct and kind, under 150 words.

### 2. Draft an SEO content brief

> **Role:** You are an SEO editor who writes briefs for freelance writers.
>
> **Task:** Create a content brief for a blog post targeting the phrase [keyword].
>
> **Context:** The reader is [who], the site sells [what], and the post should lead to [action]. Our three closest competitors' headings are inside <competitors>paste headings here</competitors>.
>
> **Rules:** Do not invent statistics or studies. Suggest sections that answer real questions, not stuffing. Mark anything that needs a source.
>
> **Output format:** Working title, search intent in one line, an outline with H2 headings, five FAQs, a list of facts that need a source.
>
> **Style:** Plain English a junior writer can follow.

### 3. Write a WhatsApp follow-up for new leads

> **Role:** You are a friendly CRM specialist for a small business.
>
> **Task:** Draft a three-message WhatsApp follow-up for someone who enquired and has not replied.
>
> **Context:** [Product or service], enquiry came from [source], typical question is [question]. Messages go out on day 1, day 3 and day 7.
>
> **Rules:** No pressure language. Do not mention discounts I have not approved. Each message must give one useful fact and one easy next step.
>
> **Output format:** Three numbered messages, each under 50 words.
>
> **Style:** Warm and conversational, English with simple Hindi words only if I ask.

### 4. Read your weekly numbers

> **Role:** You are a marketing analyst who explains numbers to non-experts.
>
> **Task:** Read the table below and tell me what changed this week and what to check first.
>
> **Context:** Goal is [goal]. Spend, clicks and leads for this week and last week are inside <data>paste table here</data>.
>
> **Rules:** Use only the numbers provided. Separate what the data shows from what you are guessing. Suggest checks, not conclusions.
>
> **Output format:** Three bullets for what changed, then a "check first" list of three items.
>
> **Style:** Short sentences, no jargon.

For a deeper example of RTCROS applied to a high-stakes setting, see our [Meta Ads MCP and CLI usage SOP](https://aiinmarketing.in/blogs/meta-ads-mcp-and-cli-sop), where the Rules section is what keeps an AI agent from spending money without approval.

## Other prompt structures worth knowing

RTCROS is one of several ways to organise a prompt. Knowing a second one helps you see what each leaves out.

**CO-STAR.** GovTech Singapore's guidance, described on the [tech.gov.sg](https://www.tech.gov.sg/media/technews/mastering-the-art-of-prompt-engineering-with-empower) site (3 April 2025), lists six components: Context, Objective, Style, Tone, Audience and Response. GovTech says its officers follow the framework in its Prompt Engineering Playbook. Here is how the two map:

| RTCROS | CO-STAR | Difference worth noticing |
|---|---|---|
| Role | (not a separate part) | RTCROS names who the AI is. |
| Task | Objective | Same job: say what you want. |
| Context | Context | Same job: background the AI cannot guess. |
| Rules | (not a separate part) | RTCROS adds do and do-not fences. |
| Output format | Response | Same job: define the shape of the answer. |
| Style | Style and Tone | CO-STAR splits voice into two. |
| (not a separate part) | Audience | In RTCROS, put the audience inside Context or Role. |

If you write for different readers all day, borrow CO-STAR's Audience line and add it to your Context. If you run an agent that can take actions, keep RTCROS's Rules.

**Examples, tags and steps.** Three techniques from Anthropic's guide work with any framework. Give a few examples of the voice or format you want. Wrap pasted material in tags so the AI can tell your instructions from your data. And split a big job into stages, where the output of one prompt becomes the input of the next. Anthropic's prompt engineering overview lists "clarity and examples", "XML structuring", "role prompting", "thinking" and "prompt chaining" among its techniques.

Our view: pick one framework, use it for two weeks and keep a note of which prompts worked. A framework you use beats a better one you forget.

## Common mistakes and quick fixes

- **Pasting too little context.** Fix: paste the real offer, the real audience and one example of work you like.
- **Asking for everything at once.** Fix: break it into steps and approve each one.
- **No rules.** Fix: add "use only the facts above" and "ask me if something is missing".
- **Accepting the first answer.** Fix: ask "what is the weakest part of this answer?" and fix it.
- **Believing confident numbers.** Fix: ask for the source or say "mark anything you cannot support". Check facts before anything is published.
- **Sharing private data.** Fix: remove names, phone numbers and client details first. Our post on [AI advertising mistakes](https://aiinmarketing.in/blogs/ai-advertising-problems-nobody-posts-about) covers data slips and unchecked claims in more detail.

## What to do this week

1. Pick one task you repeat weekly, such as ad review or a report summary.
2. Write it as an RTCROS prompt and save it in a notes app or sheet.
3. Run it on a real example and mark what you had to fix by hand.
4. Turn each fix into a Rule or a Context line, then run it again.
5. After a week you will have one reliable prompt. After a month you will have a library. That is the habit behind [vibe marketing](https://aiinmarketing.in/blogs/what-is-vibe-marketing), and the first step before you hand repeat work to an [AI agent](https://aiinmarketing.in/blogs/agentic-ai-marketing-work-competitors-hand-to-agents).

If you are a fresher, keep your best three prompts and their before-and-after outputs in a simple portfolio page. It shows an interviewer how you think, which a certificate cannot.

## How we teach prompting at AIM

In AIM we do not teach prompts as tricks to memorise. Learners use the same checklist on real tasks across the modules: SEO briefs, social content, automations and ad analysis, and trainers review the work and point out weak prompts. We have not tested RTCROS in a controlled study, so we describe it as a practical habit that works for us, not as a proven method. If you are comparing courses, our guide to [questions to ask before paying for an AI marketing course](https://aiinmarketing.in/blogs/ai-in-marketing-course-what-to-look-for) is a good starting list.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is RTCROS in prompt writing?

RTCROS is a six-part checklist for writing prompts: Role, Task, Context, Rules, Output format and Style. It is a practical habit we teach at AIM, not an official industry standard.

### Is RTCROS better than CO-STAR?

Neither is proven better. CO-STAR, described by GovTech Singapore, adds an Audience part and splits style and tone. RTCROS adds a Role and a Rules part. Pick one, use it for two weeks and keep what works.

### Can I use RTCROS with ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini?

Yes. The six parts are plain language, so they work in any chat-based AI tool. Test each tool with the same prompt because outputs differ.

### How long should a prompt be?

As long as it needs to pass the colleague test: would someone with no background understand the job? For most marketing tasks that is six short lines, plus any pasted material.

### Do I need to know coding to write good prompts?

No. You need clear thinking about the task, the audience and the rules. Basic marketing knowledge helps you judge whether the answer is good.

## Sources and how we checked them

Every source below was opened for this guide. Where a figure or quotation is used, it is attributed in the text.

- [Prompting best practices](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices), Anthropic documentation, read 3 November 2026. Used for the colleague test, role, examples and XML tag guidance.
- [Prompt engineering overview](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/overview), Anthropic documentation, read 3 November 2026. Used for the list of techniques.
- [Mastering the art of prompt engineering with Empower](https://www.tech.gov.sg/media/technews/mastering-the-art-of-prompt-engineering-with-empower), GovTech Singapore, 3 April 2025. Used for the six CO-STAR components.

**How we checked this.** The RTCROS framework itself is our own teaching checklist, so no outside source supports it as a standard. We searched for it by name and found only promotional pages that use a similar acronym with different letters, so we make no claim about its origin. The four marketing prompts are examples we wrote; the yoga workshop is a made-up brief for teaching. Tools change quickly, so test every prompt on your own account and data.

# Meta Ads MCP and CLI: A Step-by-Step Usage SOP for Marketers

URL: https://aiinmarketing.in/blogs/meta-ads-mcp-and-cli-sop
Author: Kailas Nath R
Co-author: Kautilya Roshan
Published: 2026-11-04
Summary: A step-by-step SOP for using Meta's official Ads MCP server and CLI safely: access, read-only audits, paused drafts and approvals, plus a free PDF.

Meta now offers an official Ads MCP server and a command-line tool, so an AI assistant can read your campaign data and even create ads. That is powerful and a little scary, because one careless prompt can touch real money. This guide is a plain-language SOP for Meta Ads MCP and the Ads CLI: who should have access, what to try first, and where a human must say yes.

**Key takeaways**

- Meta's Ads MCP server is Meta-hosted at https://mcp.facebook.com/ads and works with MCP-compatible AI tools. The Ads CLI is a terminal tool that wraps the Marketing API. Both are described in Meta's developer documentation.
- According to Meta's documentation, write tools create campaigns, ad sets and ads in a paused state, and activating them requires confirmation in your AI client. Treat that as a safety net, not as your only control.
- The safest order is: read-only audit, then proposals, then paused drafts, then a human activates. Never go straight to creating live ads.
- The SOP uses RTCROS prompts, so the Rules part tells the AI what it must not do, such as calling any create or activate tool during an audit.
- A free 3-page SOP document with a prerequisites checklist, five phases, prompts and a sign-off log is below, branded for AIM by Adsmentor.

## What Meta Ads MCP and the Ads CLI are

Two tools, one idea: let software talk to your Meta ad account in a controlled way.

**The Ads MCP server.** MCP stands for Model Context Protocol, an open way for AI assistants to use outside tools. Meta's developer documentation describes its Ads MCP server as a Meta-hosted server that lets you manage Meta ads from an AI agent, using "structured, permission-scoped tools". The address is https://mcp.facebook.com/ads. The documentation lists categories such as reporting, ad creation and management, catalogs, signals and datasets, A/B tests and conversion lift studies, help and troubleshooting, and activity logs.

**The Ads CLI.** CLI means command-line interface, a tool you run by typing commands. Meta's documentation says the Ads CLI wraps the Meta Marketing API so you can create campaigns, manage catalogs and Meta Pixels, and query performance insights. Commands follow a noun-verb pattern, for example meta ads campaign list.

You do not need to be a developer to use the MCP route, because you talk to an AI assistant. The CLI suits people who are comfortable in a terminal or who want repeatable scripts. Meta's overview pages we read do not label either tool as beta, though some third-party guides do, so check Meta's current documentation before you rely on either one.

## Which one should you use?

| Question | Ads MCP server | Ads CLI |
|---|---|---|
| Where does it run? | On Meta's hosted server, called by your AI client | On your computer or a server you control |
| How do you use it? | Talk to an AI assistant that supports MCP | Type commands or script them |
| Best first job | Reading and explaining performance | Repeatable lists, reports and structured creation |
| Sign-in | OAuth, user token or system user token (per Meta's docs) | System user access token (per Meta's docs) |
| Our advice | Start here, read-only | Add later for repeat tasks |

The row on sign-in matters. Meta's MCP "Get started" page lists three authentication methods: OAuth, a user access token and a system user access token. For system users it says only Employee-role tokens work: "Admin-role system user access tokens can't access the ads MCP server." The CLI "Get started" page says the CLI requires a system user access token for programmatic access.

## Before you connect anything: the ownership check

Most disasters here are not technical. They come from access nobody can trace. Before anyone connects an AI tool to an ad account, confirm four things:

1. **The business owns the ad account.** If a freelancer created it under their own profile, fix that first. Our case study on [who really owns your ad account](https://aiinmarketing.in/blogs/who-owns-your-ad-account-case-study) shows how expensive this gets.
2. **Access is least-privilege.** Give the AI connection only the permissions the job needs. For reporting, that means the read option, not management. Meta's MCP page names `ads_read` and `ads_management` among its scopes but does not label them read-only or read-write, so confirm what each allows with Meta before you rely on it.
3. **You know who the system user is.** For the CLI, Meta's setup creates a system user in Business Settings and assigns it to the app and each ad account. Write down who created it and who can revoke it.
4. **Tokens are secrets.** The CLI reads an access token from environment variables or a .env file. Keep that file out of version control and never paste a token into a chat.

## The SOP: five phases from read-only to live

The rule behind the whole procedure: the AI proposes, a human decides, and money moves only after a human says so.

### Phase 0: Set up access (30 minutes)

For the MCP route, Meta's documentation gives this command for Claude Code: claude mcp add --transport http --client-id <META_APP_ID> meta-ads https://mcp.facebook.com/ads. A Meta developer app is optional according to the page; without one, Meta points to a separate setup in its help centre. For the CLI route, Meta lists Homebrew (brew tap facebook/fb, brew trust facebook/fb, brew install facebook/fb/meta-ads) or pip install meta-ads, then a system user token. Run meta auth status to confirm the setup and meta ads adaccount list to find your account.

Official documentation and some third-party guides disagree on the CLI package name and sign-in method. We follow Meta's developer documentation. Check the page again on the day you install, because tools like this change quickly.

### Phase 1: Read-only audit

Ask the AI to read, never to change. Meta's reporting tools include ads_get_ad_entities (campaigns, ad sets and ads with spend, impressions, CTR, CPC, CPM and conversions), ads_insights_performance_trend, ads_insights_anomaly_signal and ads_get_opportunity_score. Here is an RTCROS prompt for it. The account details are an example brief, not a real client.

> **Role:** You are a senior paid social analyst who explains findings to a business owner.
>
> **Task:** Audit the last 30 days of this Meta ad account and tell me what is working, what is wasting money and what to check first.
>
> **Context:** Online saree store in Pune, goal is purchases at a return on ad spend above 3. Monthly budget about ₹60,000. Use the ad account I connected.
>
> **Rules:** Read-only. Do not call any tool that creates, updates, activates or deletes anything. Use only data returned by the tools. If a number is missing, say so. Do not guess reasons; list them as hypotheses.
>
> **Output format:** Three sections: working, wasting money, check first. Add a table of top five campaigns by spend with spend, purchases and return on ad spend.
>
> **Style:** Plain English, short sentences, no jargon.

### Phase 2: Check what changed and who changed it

Many bad weeks start with a change nobody remembers. Meta's activity logs tool, ads_account_get_activity_logs, retrieves log entries for an ad account and can be narrowed by object, time window, event category or user. Ask for the last two weeks of changes before you decide why performance moved. If the log shows edits by someone who should not have access, fix access before you fix ads.

### Phase 3: Ask for proposals, not actions

Now ask the AI to propose structural changes, such as a new ad set or a different audience, in words. You approve or reject each one. Keep the Rules strict:

> **Role:** You are a media planner proposing changes for approval.
>
> **Task:** Propose up to three changes for next week and explain the expected benefit and the risk of each.
>
> **Context:** Use the audit from phase 1 and the activity log from phase 2.
>
> **Rules:** Do not execute anything. State which tool or command each change would need. Mark anything that restarts learning or changes budget.
>
> **Output format:** A numbered list with: change, reason, risk, tool needed.
>
> **Style:** Short and specific.

### Phase 4: Create drafts, always paused

Only after you approve a proposal should the AI create anything. Meta's documentation for the MCP creation tools (ads_create_campaign, ads_create_ad_set, ads_create_ad) says write tools create entities in a paused state and that your AI client asks for confirmation before activation. Its ads_activate_entity tool switches a paused campaign, ad set or ad to active, which starts spending budget. The CLI tutorial likewise says everything is created in PAUSED status by default, so nothing spends until you activate each level.

> **Role:** You are an assistant that prepares campaign drafts for a human to review.
>
> **Task:** Create the approved campaign as a draft.
>
> **Context:** Approved change number 2 from phase 3: [paste the approved change, objective, budget and audience].
>
> **Rules:** Create everything paused. Show me the exact tool call or command before you run it and wait for me to type APPROVE. Never call an activate tool or set any status to active. If any detail is unclear, ask.
>
> **Output format:** After creating, list each object with its name, ID and status.
>
> **Style:** Concise.

A units check before real budgets. Meta's CLI tutorial uses --daily-budget 5000 in its example but does not explain the unit on the page we read. Test on a practice account and confirm in the command reference how budget values are interpreted before you enter a real amount.

### Phase 5: Review, activate by hand, then log

A human opens the draft in Ads Manager, checks the creative, audience, placements, budget and links, and then activates in order: campaign, ad set, ad. The CLI tutorial gives the same order. Record who approved it, when and why in your sign-off log. A week later, run the phase 1 audit again to compare.

## Safety rules we would add to any team

- **Separate reading from writing.** Use a read-only connection for audits, and a separate connection for creation that few people can use.
- **Be careful with --force and --no-input.** Meta's tutorial notes these flags suppress prompts, so a script can delete resources with no confirmation. It also says deleting a campaign deletes its ad sets and ads. Never put delete commands in an automated job until you have tested them on dummy data.
- **Use the official server.** Third-party Meta ads servers exist. Because they would hold the keys to your ad account, evaluate them like any vendor with account access, and prefer the official route.
- **Keep a human on money.** Do not use an AI loop for anything time-critical, and do not let it activate spend by itself.
- **Check logs weekly.** Use the activity log to catch unplanned changes.
- **Protect secrets.** Keep tokens and the .env file out of shared folders and out of chats.

## A short command cheat sheet from Meta's documentation

These commands come from the Ads CLI pages. Replace values in angle brackets.

| Job | Command |
|---|---|
| Check setup | meta auth status |
| List ad accounts | meta ads adaccount list |
| List campaigns | meta ads campaign list |
| Get performance | meta ads insights get --fields spend,impressions,ctr,cpc |
| List campaigns as JSON | meta --output json ads campaign list |
| Activate (human step) | meta ads campaign update <CAMPAIGN_ID> --status ACTIVE |

Global options such as --output go before the subcommand, and the documentation lists exit codes from 0 for success to 5 for not found. Settings resolve in this order: command-line flags, then environment variables, then the project .env file.

## What this does not do for you

The tools give an AI assistant access. They do not supply strategy, creative taste or judgement about your customers, and they do not make a weak offer perform. They also do not remove your responsibility for what runs: the advertiser is still accountable for claims and policy. The most useful AI help we see in ad accounts is investigation and reporting, which is the work phases 1 and 2 cover. Our guide on [staying in control as ad accounts automate](https://aiinmarketing.in/blogs/ad-accounts-run-themselves) explains which decisions should stay with you, and our list of [AI advertising mistakes](https://aiinmarketing.in/blogs/ai-advertising-problems-nobody-posts-about) includes automation that spends without approval.

## What to do this week

1. Check ownership of your ad account and list who has access today.
2. Read Meta's MCP "Get started" page and decide whether you need the MCP route, the CLI route or neither yet.
3. Connect read-only and run the phase 1 audit on a practice or low-spend account.
4. Save the RTCROS prompts from this guide in your notes. If prompt writing is new to you, start with our [RTCROS prompt guide](https://aiinmarketing.in/blogs/rtcros-prompt-framework-for-marketers).
5. Write your sign-off log: date, person, change, reason and result.

If you are a fresher or career switcher, a documented SOP like this one is a strong portfolio piece. It shows you can use AI tools and respect client money.

## Where AIM fits

In AIM, learners work in real ad platforms and practise reading, proposing and reviewing before they spend. Trainers review the work, and portfolio ad spend is included so you practise on real campaigns. We do not promise jobs. We teach a working method, and this SOP is the way we think about AI in an ad account: the AI can help, the person decides.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is the Meta Ads MCP server?

It is a Meta-hosted Model Context Protocol server at https://mcp.facebook.com/ads that lets an MCP-compatible AI assistant read and manage Meta ad data through permission-scoped tools, according to Meta's developer documentation.

### What is the difference between Meta Ads MCP and the Ads CLI?

The MCP server lets an AI assistant use Meta ad tools through conversation. The CLI is a terminal tool where you or a script type commands. Meta's documentation describes both as ways to work with the Marketing API.

### Will the AI spend my money without asking?

Meta's documentation says write tools create campaigns, ad sets and ads in a paused state and that your AI client asks for confirmation before activation. Still, add your own rule: a human activates every ad.

### Do I need to know coding to use Meta Ads MCP?

Not for the MCP route, since you talk to an AI assistant, though setup involves OAuth or tokens. The CLI is comfortable only if you can work in a terminal.

### Is it safe to connect an AI tool to my ad account?

It can be if you follow least privilege, start read-only, keep tokens secret, review the activity log and keep human approval on spend. Use the official server rather than unknown third-party ones.

# Duolingo's AI-First Memo, 18 Months On: What Its Own Filings Show

URL: https://aiinmarketing.in/blogs/duolingo-ai-first-case-study-18-months-on
Author: Kailas Nath R
Co-author: Kautilya Roshan
Published: 2026-11-04
Summary: What happened after Duolingo's April 2025 AI-first memo, from its own SEC letters: output, users, costs and trust, plus a free AI announcement checklist.

In April 2025 one all-hands email ended with Duolingo wiping its TikTok and Instagram posts. Eighteen months later, Duolingo's own shareholder letters let us check what followed the Duolingo AI-first memo: how much more content it makes, what AI costs it, whether users kept coming and what it says about trust. This case study separates what the filings prove from what they do not, and turns it into steps for marketers and small business owners.

**Key takeaways**

- On 28 April 2025 Duolingo's CEO told staff the company would be "AI-first" and would "gradually stop using contractors to do work that AI can handle". The backlash was about people, not about the technology.
- Duolingo's Q1 2026 letter says it published 20,500 course units in one quarter, against 7,100 per quarter in 2025 and 1,800 per quarter in 2024, and credits AI tools for the change.
- Daily users kept growing in the company's own numbers: 50.5 million in Q3 2025 and 64.9 million in Q3 2026. The letters do not credit or blame the memo for that, and neither should we.
- The company's own explanations point to monetisation friction and a quieter brand voice as reasons growth slowed in 2025, which is a lesson in itself: sentiment and sales are separate ledgers.
- Before you announce AI to a team, freelancers or customers, run the four-audience check below. A free 3-page checklist is included.

## The short version

Duolingo told its staff on 28 April 2025 that it would be "AI-first". People heard "the company will replace its workers with AI". The CEO later said he had not given enough context. Since then its shareholder letters show three things at once: AI really did multiply Duolingo's content output, users kept growing, and the company chose to spend part of its growth budget on trust and word of mouth.

None of that proves the memo helped or hurt. What it gives you is a rare, well-documented example of a brand announcing AI in public, which is exactly the decision many small businesses and agencies are making now, with far less scrutiny.

## Timeline: April 2025 to November 2026

| Date | What happened | Source |
|---|---|---|
| 28 April 2025 | CEO Luis von Ahn emails staff, and the memo is posted on Duolingo's LinkedIn page. | [Snopes via Yahoo](https://www.yahoo.com/news/fact-check-duolingo-said-become-100000452.html), 6 May 2025 |
| 30 April 2025 | Duolingo announces 148 new courses made with generative AI. | [TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2025/04/30/duolingo-launches-148-courses-created-with-ai-after-sharing-plans-to-replace-contractors-with-ai/), 30 April 2025 |
| By 22 May 2025 | Duolingo has wiped its TikTok and Instagram posts. | [YPulse](https://www.ypulse.com/newsfeed/2025/05/22/duolingo-deleted-their-instagram-and-tiktok-posts-after-getting-backlash-over-ai/), 22 May 2025 |
| 23 May 2025 | The CEO posts a clarification on LinkedIn. | [Entrepreneur](https://www.entrepreneur.com/business-news/duolingo-ceo-clarifies-ai-stance-after-backlash-read-memo/492141), 23 May 2025 |
| 6 August 2025 | On the earnings call he says he "didn't give enough context". | [TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2025/08/07/the-backlash-against-duolingo-going-ai-first-didnt-even-matter/), 7 August 2025 |
| November 2025 | Q3 letter: daily users 50.5 million, up 36 percent. | [Duolingo Q3 2025 letter](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1562088/000162828025049514/q3fy25duolingo9-30x25share.htm), SEC |
| February 2026 | Q4 letter sets a 100 million daily user goal for 2028 and a shift towards the free experience. | [Duolingo Q4 2025 letter](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1562088/000162828026012246/q4fy25duolingo12-31x25shar.htm), SEC |
| May 2026 | Q1 letter reports 20,500 course units in a quarter. | [Duolingo Q1 2026 letter](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001562088/000162828026029790/q1fy26duolingo3-31x26share.htm), SEC |
| 3 November 2026 | Q3 letter: daily users 64.9 million, up 29 percent. | [Duolingo Q3 2026 letter](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001562088/000162828026069474/q3fy26duolingo9-30x26share.htm), SEC |

The dates in the first five rows come from press reports. The 6 August 2025 earnings call date is inferred from TechCrunch's report published on 7 August. For the last four rows the company's own letters are the source, which makes them the strongest evidence in this story.

## What the memo actually promised

Snopes reproduced the key lines of the all-hands email in its fact check. According to that fact check, the memo said:

> "Duolingo is going to be AI-first."
>
> "We'll gradually stop using contractors to do work that AI can handle"
>
> "AI use will be part of what we look for in hiring"
>
> "AI use will be part of what we evaluate in performance reviews"
>
> "Headcount will only be given if a team cannot automate more of their work"

Fortune, reporting on the memo on 30 April 2025, quoted a line about trade-offs: the company would rather "take occasional small hits on quality than move slowly and miss the moment". The same report says the memo's reason for the change was to overcome human limits in producing the large volume of content Duolingo needs.

Read it as an employee or a freelance translator and one line stands out: the contractor line. Read it as an investor and a different line stands out: the output. A single message is read by several audiences at once, and each one hears the part that affects them.

## The backlash and the clarification

Two days after the memo, TechCrunch reported the 148 new courses. It also repeated Duolingo's own contrast: developing its first 100 courses "took about 12 years", while nearly 150 more arrived in about a year. The proof of benefit was real. It just landed next to a sentence about contractors.

In May, according to YPulse (which credits Ad Age), Duolingo removed all of its posts from TikTok and Instagram. We could not open the Ad Age or Fast Company reports, and published follower-loss figures differ between outlets, so we leave them out.

On 23 May, Entrepreneur published the CEO's LinkedIn clarification. He wrote: "One of the most important things leaders can do is provide clarity." And: "When I released my AI memo a few weeks ago, I didn't do that well." He added: "To be clear: I do not see AI as replacing what our employees do", and said the company was "continuing to hire at the same speed as before". PR Daily reported on 28 May that Duolingo also promised workshops, advisory councils and time for staff to experiment.

Fortune quoted him again on 18 August 2025, citing a New York Times interview: "This was on me. I did not give enough context", and "We've never laid off any full-time employees. We don't plan to." We did not open the Times interview itself, so treat these as Fortune's reporting of it.

Notice the order: the proof came first, the reassurance came about four weeks later, and the specifics (hiring, training, workshops) came last. Most small businesses can reverse that order.

## What the filings show: the scoreboard

Shareholder letters are the safest numbers in this story because the company files them with the US securities regulator. We opened four of them and checked every number below against the letter named. Here is what they say, with the letter named in each row.

| Measure | What the letter says | Letter |
|---|---|---|
| Content output | 1,800 course units per quarter in 2024, 7,100 per quarter in 2025, 20,500 in Q1 2026, "by investing in AI tools" | Q1 2026 |
| Daily users | 50.5 million in Q3 2025, up 36 percent | Q3 2025 |
| Daily users | 64.9 million in Q3 2026, up 29 percent, after 23 percent in Q2 | Q3 2026 |
| Paid subscribers | 13.1 million in Q3 2026, up 14 percent | Q3 2026 |
| Revenue | $309.0 million in Q3 2026, up 14 percent | Q3 2026 |
| Gross margin | Q3 2025 fell about 40 basis points "as a result of increases in generative AI and hosting costs" | Q3 2025 |
| Gross margin | Q1 2026 rose to 73.0%, "driven primarily by continued reductions in per-unit AI costs" | Q1 2026 |
| Gross margin outlook | About 69% for the rest of 2026 (February), then 72.0% expected for Q4 (November) | Q4 2025, Q3 2026 |

Three observations a marketer can use.

**AI scale is real, and so is the bill.** The same letters that celebrate faster content creation also list AI as a cost. Gross margin moved with AI use and AI unit costs. If you add AI to your service, price for the cost you will actually carry.

**Output is not quality.** The Q1 2026 letter says automation also lets Duolingo push changes across many courses at once and improve quality more consistently. That is the company's claim. We did not test the courses, and it adds that this is "already improving engagement among new users".

**Users kept coming.** Daily users rose from 50.5 million to 64.9 million between the Q3 2025 and Q3 2026 letters. TechCrunch's August 2025 headline said the backlash "didn't even matter" for the business, and the later numbers fit that. They do not prove it, as the next section explains.

## What these numbers do not prove

It is tempting to read the user growth as proof that the backlash was noise. We would not. The company's letters give other explanations.

- The Q4 2025 letter says: "we believe that this extra friction is part of the reason our DAU growth has slowed", meaning ads and subscription upsells. Duolingo decided to "prioritize user growth over monetization", estimating more than $50 million of foregone bookings, or about 5 points of bookings growth.
- The Q3 2025 letter says growth was slower than the quarter before "in part because we posted less 'unhinged' content on our English-speaking social media accounts as we listened to community feedback and prioritized building long-term brand sentiment". It adds that the company later "started posting more unhinged content" and saw a significant increase in impressions.
- The Q3 2026 letter says the company "laid out a plan to prioritize teaching better and user growth, knowing it would take time to see results".

So the honest reading is this. The company did change its brand behaviour after the backlash, and it did choose to trade some revenue for goodwill and growth. It never says in these letters that the memo caused any of it. One company, one period, many moving parts: this is a case study, not an experiment.

## Five lessons for marketers and small business owners

**1. Treat an AI announcement as four conversations.** Your team, your freelancers, your customers and the public each need different first sentences. The memo's reader list was long; the message was one paragraph.

**2. Lead with the people line.** If the work of freelancers or staff changes, say what stays, what changes and by when, before you talk about speed. Duolingo's clearest reassurance (hiring, training, no layoffs of full-time staff) arrived last.

**3. Put your clarification on a calendar.** The CEO's own words were that leaders should "provide clarity". Decide in advance when you will follow up (see the 30-day plan in the checklist), and put one named person in charge of the answers.

**4. Match your response to your brand's character.** A playful brand that goes quiet sends a message too. Duolingo's own letter says it later went back to posting more of its playful content and saw impressions rise. Decide beforehand whether your usual voice still fits a serious moment.

**5. Track sentiment next to sales.** Duolingo's letters talk about brand sentiment and word of mouth in the same breath as bookings. For a small business that can be as simple as tracking replies, comments, reviews and unsubscribes after an announcement, week by week.

Our post on [AI advertising mistakes](https://aiinmarketing.in/blogs/ai-advertising-problems-nobody-posts-about) covers the client side of disclosure in more detail, and our guide to [vibe marketing](https://aiinmarketing.in/blogs/what-is-vibe-marketing) explains why teams that talk openly about how they use AI learn faster.

## If you run a small business or freelance in India

You do not need a memo. You need a plain statement, once, in the right order.

- **Freelance designers, writers and video editors you use:** tell them first, privately. Say which tasks AI will help with, which work stays with them, and when you will review that. A short, early message is kinder than a surprise in an invoice cycle.
- **Clients:** say what AI does in your process and who checks it. Many clients value that honesty, as we note in our guide on [handing work to AI agents](https://aiinmarketing.in/blogs/agentic-ai-marketing-work-competitors-hand-to-agents).
- **Customers:** if AI writes anything customers read, such as replies, descriptions or ads, a human should approve it before it goes out.
- **Freshers and career switchers:** a one-page note on how you use AI, what you check and what you never delegate is a stronger interview exhibit than "I know ChatGPT".

## The ten-minute test before you post

Answer each question in writing before you announce a change in how you use AI:

1. Who is affected, by name or by group?
2. What will not change for each of them?
3. What will change, and by what date?
4. Who will answer questions, and where?
5. What proof can I show that quality is protected?
6. Would I be comfortable if this message were posted publicly tomorrow?
7. Which sentence will a worried person read first?
8. Have I told the most affected people before everyone else?
9. When will I follow up, and what will I report?
10. Which numbers will I watch for 30 days?

The PDF below puts this into a one-page planner with a statement template.

## What to do this week

1. List everyone affected by how you use AI today.
2. Write the 120-word statement from the checklist, and read it aloud as a freelancer would hear it.
3. Tell the most affected person privately before you tell anyone else.
4. Put the follow-up dates in your calendar.
5. Choose three numbers (replies, reviews, unsubscribes) and note where they are today.

## How we think about this at AIM

In AIM we teach learners to use AI in real marketing work and to be open about it: which tasks AI did, what a person checked and what was changed. We learned from cases like this one that the technology is rarely the hard part. If you are weighing training options, our list of [questions to ask before paying for an AI marketing course](https://aiinmarketing.in/blogs/ai-in-marketing-course-what-to-look-for) is a good place to start.

## Frequently asked questions

### What did the Duolingo AI-first memo say?

According to Snopes, the 28 April 2025 all-hands email said Duolingo would be "AI-first", would "gradually stop using contractors to do work that AI can handle", and that AI use would be part of hiring and performance reviews. Headcount would only be given if a team could not automate more of its work.

### Did Duolingo lay off employees because of AI?

In an interview reported by Fortune on 18 August 2025, CEO Luis von Ahn said, "We've never laid off any full-time employees. We don't plan to." He said the contractor force goes up and down with needs. We did not open the original interview.

### Did the backlash hurt Duolingo's business?

Duolingo's own letters show daily users rising from 50.5 million in Q3 2025 to 64.9 million in Q3 2026. The letters give other reasons for slower growth in 2025, such as monetisation friction and posting less playful social content, and they do not link the memo to results. One company over one period cannot prove cause and effect.

### How much more content does Duolingo make with AI?

The Q1 2026 letter says Duolingo published 20,500 course units in the quarter, up from 7,100 per quarter in 2025 and 1,800 per quarter in 2024, and credits investment in AI tools. We did not independently test the content.

### Should a small business tell customers it uses AI?

In our view yes, plainly and once: say what AI helps with and who checks it. Tell the people most affected, such as freelancers, before you tell everyone else.

## Sources and how we checked them

Every source below was opened for this case study. Quotations and numbers are attributed in the text to the page that states them.

- [Duolingo Q3 2025 shareholder letter](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1562088/000162828025049514/q3fy25duolingo9-30x25share.htm), SEC filing, November 2025. Daily users, "unhinged" content passage, generative AI cost note.
- [Duolingo Q4 and full-year 2025 shareholder letter](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1562088/000162828026012246/q4fy25duolingo12-31x25shar.htm), SEC filing, February 2026. Friction trade-off, word of mouth, 2028 goal and 2026 outlook.
- [Duolingo Q1 2026 shareholder letter](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001562088/000162828026029790/q1fy26duolingo3-31x26share.htm), SEC filing, May 2026. Course units, revenue and gross margin.
- [Duolingo Q3 2026 shareholder letter](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001562088/000162828026069474/q3fy26duolingo9-30x26share.htm), SEC filing, 3 November 2026. Daily users, subscribers, revenue and strategy.
- [Fact check: Duolingo said it would become AI-first](https://www.yahoo.com/news/fact-check-duolingo-said-become-100000452.html), Snopes via Yahoo, 6 May 2025. Memo quotations and date.
- [Duolingo launches 148 courses created with AI](https://techcrunch.com/2025/04/30/duolingo-launches-148-courses-created-with-ai-after-sharing-plans-to-replace-contractors-with-ai/), TechCrunch, 30 April 2025.
- [Duolingo CEO says getting rid of contract employees](https://www.fortune.com/article/duolingo-ceo-says-getting-rid-of-contract-employees-replacing-them-with-ai), Fortune, 30 April 2025. Quality trade-off line.
- [Duolingo deleted their Instagram and TikTok posts](https://www.ypulse.com/newsfeed/2025/05/22/duolingo-deleted-their-instagram-and-tiktok-posts-after-getting-backlash-over-ai/), YPulse, 22 May 2025. Posts removed (credited there to Ad Age).
- [Duolingo CEO clarifies AI stance after backlash: read the memo](https://www.entrepreneur.com/business-news/duolingo-ceo-clarifies-ai-stance-after-backlash-read-memo/492141), Entrepreneur, 23 May 2025.
- [The Scoop: Duolingo CEO walks back AI-first memo](https://www.prdaily.com/the-scoop-duolingo-ceo-walks-back-ai-first-memo/), PR Daily, 28 May 2025.
- [The backlash against Duolingo going AI-first didn't even matter](https://techcrunch.com/2025/08/07/the-backlash-against-duolingo-going-ai-first-didnt-even-matter/), TechCrunch, 7 August 2025.
- [Duolingo CEO admits controversial AI memo did not give enough context](https://fortune.com/2025/08/18/duolingo-ceo-admits-controversial-ai-memo-did-not-give-enough-context-insists-company-never-laid-off-full-time-employees), Fortune, 18 August 2025.

**What we tested and what we did not.** We opened each source above and read the passages we quote. We compared numbers across four shareholder letters and checked every figure in the scoreboard against the letter named. We did not test Duolingo's product or courses, did not open the New York Times interview, the original LinkedIn post, or the Ad Age and Fast Company reports (they block automated access), and did not use follower-loss numbers because outlets disagree. The memo date is from Snopes; Morning Brew's report suggests the email went out a day later, so treat the day as approximate. The article says nothing about causes that the sources do not state.
